practices.title: Information and code length are different quantities
practices.prompt: A source has five labels with probabilities (1/2,1/8,1/8,1/8,1/8). Calculate its entropy and construct a prefix code attaining it. Compare fixed-width coding and the actual message AEEE. Explain why a 2.5-bit message average would not contradict the 2-bit source entropy.
practices.hint: Use the five masses 1/2,1/8,1/8,1/8,1/8. A code may finish at one leaf while the other branch contains a complete two-level subtree.
practices.solution: The entropy is (1/2)×1+4×(1/8)×3=2 bits per symbol. One optimal prefix code is A=0, B=100, C=101, D=110, E=111, with average 2. Fixed-width coding needs three bits for five labels. Message AEEE uses 1+3+3+3=10 bits, or 2.5 per symbol, exceeding the source entropy on that message. Entropy predicts a source-weighted average, not a per-message guarantee.

practices.title: Compute a changed mismatch and diagnose the signed terms
practices.prompt: For P=(3/4,1/4) and Q=(1/2,1/2), compute entropy, cross-entropy, both signed KL contributions and the reverse KL. Explain why taking the absolute value of each contribution would define a different quantity.
practices.hint: The uniform model charges one bit per outcome. Keep P=(3/4,1/4) as the weighting distribution.
practices.solution: Compute H₂(P) as −(3/4)log₂(3/4) − (1/4)log₂(1/4), obtaining about 0.811278 bits. H₂(P,Q)=1, so KL≈0.188722 bits. The terms are (3/4)log₂(3/2)≈0.438722 and (1/4)log₂(1/2)=−0.25. The negative term says the rarer outcome is priced more cheaply by Q; it is not a negative divergence on its own. Reversing gives about 0.207519 bits, so the direction matters.

practices.title: Decode a changed stream and reject an ambiguous code
practices.prompt: Decode 110010111 using the lesson's matched code. Then inspect A=0, B=00, C=1. Give a concrete ambiguous bitstream and explain why “always choose the shortest matching word” is not a repair.
practices.hint: Start again at the root each time 0,10,110 or 111 is complete. For the proposed code, ask whether 00 could mean more than one message.
practices.solution: Using A=0, B=10, C=110, D=111, the stream 110010111 decodes C A B D: 110|0|10|111. The alternative A=0, B=00, C=1 is not prefix-free and is not uniquely decodable: 00 could mean B or AA. A decoder that simply chooses the shortest match loses B. A correct changed implementation must reject that code and also reject a final unfinished 11 under the original code.

practices.title: Repair a support and clipping claim
practices.prompt: For P=(0.8,0.2,0) and Q=(1,0,0), classify both KL directions. A colleague replaces log 0 with log 10⁻⁶ and reports “the exact original KL.” Explain the error and give one valid explicitly smoothed model.
practices.hint: Check the support inclusion separately in each direction. A probability floor must come with a defined normalized model.
practices.solution: For P=(0.8,0.2,0) and Q=(1,0,0), KL(P∥Q)=∞ because the second outcome occurs under P but is excluded by Q. KL(Q∥P)=−log₂0.8≈0.321928 bits. Reporting a finite clipped loss does not establish finite KL for the original Q. One explicit replacement is Q_ε=(1−2ε,ε,ε), 0<ε<1/2; it is a new normalized distribution, and its score should be identified as such. No contribution is charged for P's zero third coordinate.

practices.title: Use unequal context frequencies
practices.prompt: P(X=0)=0.75, P(Y=1|X=0)=0.2 and P(Y=1|X=1)=0.8. Calculate H(Y), H(Y|X), and the ideal expected losses with and without X. Explain which probabilities would need changing if the context frequencies shifted.
practices.hint: Average the two conditional entropies with 0.75 and 0.25. First calculate the marginal probability of Y=1.
practices.solution: P(Y=1)=0.75×0.2+0.25×0.8=0.35, so H(Y)=h₂(0.35)≈0.934068 bits. Both contexts have entropy h₂(0.2)=h₂(0.8)≈0.721928, hence H(Y|X)=0.721928. A model that uses the true conditional achieves that expected loss. A model using the true marginal in both contexts has expected loss 0.934068. The context's average reduction is about 0.212140 bits. Weighting the contexts equally would generally be wrong, even though this symmetric pair happens to have equal conditional entropies.

practices.title: Evaluate confidence with a consistent denominator
practices.prompt: On six shared binary test cases, C's correct-label probabilities are (0.9,0.9,0.9,0.9,0.4,0.4). D's are (0.6,0.6,0.6,0.6,0.6,0.01). Calculate accuracy and mean log loss. Which wins each measure, and what additional claim would this small test not justify?
practices.hint: Use all six correct-label probabilities. Model C has four probabilities above 0.5, while D has five.
practices.solution: C has accuracy 4/6 and mean loss −[4ln0.9+2ln0.4]/6≈0.375671 nats. D has accuracy 5/6 and mean loss −[5ln0.6+ln0.01]/6≈1.193216 nats. D wins accuracy but loses log loss because its lone error is extremely confident. The difference does not certify fairness, calibration or performance after distribution shift. A defensible comparison states the same six cases, binary threshold/no ties, arithmetic mean over cases and the decision objective.

practices.title: Compute an extreme but finite log loss
practices.prompt: Scores are (800,0,−800), and the last class occurs. Calculate the stable loss and explain why adding −700 to every score changes nothing. Give both an ordinary-score acceptance case and an underflow case for an implementation test.
practices.hint: Subtract the maximum first. The normalizer's log is approximately zero when the remaining exponentials underflow.
practices.solution: For scores (800,0,−800), shifted scores are (0,−800,−1600). The observed last-class loss is 1600+ln(1+e⁻⁸⁰⁰+e⁻¹⁶⁰⁰), numerically 1600 nats in the displayed precision. Adding −700 to every score leaves it unchanged. Taking log of a separately underflowed zero probability gives ∞ and destroys a finite-logit result. At ordinary scores (1,0,−1), direct and stable calculations should agree within tolerance; that is a useful independent implementation check.

practices.title: Preserve the physical experiment when changing units
practices.prompt: X is uniform on [0,2] metres. Express its differential entropy in metres and millimetres; quantize it into four equal bins and compare bin-label entropy. Then explain why finite negative log density on observed samples does not establish finite KL from their empirical point-mass distribution.
practices.hint: Uniform width w has differential entropy log₂w. An aligned bin label has entropy log₂N.
practices.solution: For a uniform interval of width 2 metres, h₂=1. In millimetres the numerical width is 2000, so h₂=log₂2000≈10.965784; the change is log₂1000. Four equal bins have H=2 bits in both units. Their widths are 0.5 m and 500 mm, so h−log₂Δ=2 either way. The probability of the first physical metre is 1/2 in both coordinates. For a continuous Q, the empirical finite set remains Q-null despite positive density at observed points; empirical-to-Q measure KL is ∞, while average negative log density can be finite.

practices.title: Certify a new constrained maximum
practices.prompt: On outcomes 0,1,2, replace the required mean with 1/2. Derive the feasible slice, find the positive exponential-family candidate and prove it maximizes entropy. State what changes if the base weights become (1,2,1).
practices.hint: For mean 1/2, q=(1/2+t,1/2−2t,t), 0≤t≤1/4. Put candidate probabilities proportional to 1,r,r² and solve their mean equation.
practices.solution: The equation (r+2r²)/(1+r+r²)=1/2 gives 3r²+r−1=0, with positive root r=(√13−1)/6. Normalize (1,r,r²) to get approximately (0.616204,0.267592,0.116204). Its mean is 1/2. The candidate's log probability is x ln r−ln(1+r+r²); every feasible q has the same expected log price. Thus KL(q∥p*)=H(p*)−H(q)≥0 and equality requires q=p*. Checking only the derivative or only a sampled plot would not by itself supply this global certificate. A base h=(1,2,1) would add E_q log h to the certified objective.

checkpoints.prompt: A model assigns probability 1 to A. What is the information in seeing A? What would seeing B reveal if P(B)=0?
checkpoints.solution: A has −log₂1=0 bits: it was completely predicted. B has infinite model surprise; its occurrence contradicts the model's exclusion of B. That does not prove B is impossible in reality. It exposes a model-support error.

checkpoints.prompt: P=(1,0) and Q=(1/2,1/2). Someone says their supports differ, so both KL directions must be infinite. Repair the claim.
checkpoints.solution: KL(P∥Q)=log₂2=1 bit: Q assigns positive probability to P's only possible outcome. KL(Q∥P)=∞ because Q sometimes draws the second outcome that P excludes. Different supports alone do not settle finiteness; the direction of the inclusion matters.
